state: We sampled corrosion scale from forty coastal bridge girders and profiled pit depth against weld heat-affected zone grain size under SEM.

went out with the district health team for elevn days to survey three villages after the cholera cluster started. we used a phone app with a convolutional neural net to score photos of household water jars as clean, cloudy or visibly contaminated, which honestly worked pretty well and saved us a ton of time compared to lab turbidity tests. but the real work was the case count. we interviewed 412 households, recorded 61 confirmed cases by rapid test and matched them against three exposure variables: distance to the nearest borehole, whether the household boiled water before drinking, and whether a pit latrine sat uphill of their well. attack rate in the uphill-latrine group was almost four times higher than the rest, 28% vs 7%, and the boiling variable barely moved the numbers once we controlled for that. the photo classifier flagged some jars as clean that were actually fine bacteriologically, so we're not leaning on it for the final risk model, just using it to triage which wells get retested first. writing this up for the district office tomorow, main finding is latrine placement relative to the well, not water appearance, is driving who gets sick. recomending relocation of six wells before the rains start again next month.

spent the week collecting bark and resin samples from wild conifer stands up in the ridge country, forty two trees across six stands. back in the shed we ran crude extracts through column chromatography and picked off three resin acids that came out cleaner than the usual pine rosin fractions. tried an esterification on the biggest fraction with methanol and a acid catalyst, got about 78% conversion by NMR integration, yield's decent but the reaction still throws off a stubborn side product we cant identify yet. gonna send the NMR and IR traces to the lab in town next week, see if they can pin down the functional group thats fouling the ester step.

In this study we undertake an exhaustive reanalysis of sixty-two years of gridded surface temperature, precipitation, and sea-level pressure records spanning 1962 to 2024, drawing on billions of station-days merged with satellite-era corrections for instrument drift. Our aim is to quantify how anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing, aerosol loading, and large-scale ocean oscillations such as the Pacific Decadal Oscillation have jointly shaped regional warming trends across six continents. Using an ensemble of thirty-one general circulation models alongside the observational reanalysis, we detect a robust acceleration in tropospheric warming since 1998 that internal variability alone cannot explain, attributing roughly seventy percent of the post-2000 trend to rising atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.
we hiked to all nine underground mine-shaft stations this week to service the muon counters, and honestly the coincidence rate at the deepest site was so much cleaner than up at the surface hut!

My grandfather spent forty years running lathes at the shipyard, and he used to say a blade either 'wants to crack' or it doesn't, long before anyone could explain why. I've been thinking about him a lot while running our latest set of simulations, where we let atoms in a nickel-based lattice hop around a vacancy for a few million timesteps to see how a stacking fault nucleates under shear. The energy barrier we compute for dislocation glide past a coherent precipitate keeps landing right where the old fatigue-crack initiation sites used to show up on the turbine blades he used to machine, which is a strange thing to sit with.

We validate a paper-strip assay detecting three arboviral pathogens from a single fingerstick, tested against 1,200 outbreak-surveillance specimens with 94% case-detection sensitivity in resource-limited clinics.

Every few years someone publishes a tidy chart claiming the vowels of a certain valley town have shifted a full step in one generation, and every few years I find myself squinting at their sample size. This synthesis works through eleven such generational comparisons from small communities, and frankly only four hold up once you account for how the recordings were elicited — reading a word list into a microphone is not the same as ordering coffee. What survives the cull is a modest but real drift in how young speakers round a handful of back vowels, nothing like the dramatic reinventions the headlines promised.

so this week was a mess honestly. truck wouldnt start monday, spent three hours with jumper cables in the parking lot before georgia showed up with her truck to boost us. then wednesday it rained sideways the entire day and we just sat in the van eating stale crackers and arguing about whether the radio station out here is even real or just static with a beat. thursday was better, sun came out, we fixed the broken cooler latch with a bungee cord and some duct tape, classic field camp fix. friday marco brought his dog again even though hes not supposed to, dog chased a rabbit into the brush and we lost him for twenty minutes, everyone was yelling his name across the whole ridge. anyway in between all that we did manage to deploy the new automated camera-trap array we built, it snaps a photo every time a flower head moves more than two centimeters, which lets us log pollinator visitation rates on the shrub plots without a human sitting there for six hours straight, and it caught way more bee and moth visits per hour than our old manual counts ever did, which is going to change how we estimate seed set for the whole population next season. after that we mostly just packed up, ate some of marcos leftover trail mix as a joke, and drove back into town for real food and showers, which we badly needed after four days out there.

My aunt worked contact tracing during flu seasons when I was a kid, and she always said the hardest part wasn't finding cases, it was guessing who they'd already infected before anyone looked. That's basically the problem our new compartmental model solves: we let the reproduction number vary by neighborhood density and household size, then run the system forward to see how fast a respiratory pathogen moves through a mid-sized city before symptomatic reporting catches up. Early runs suggest that by the time official case counts double, the true infected pool is already six to eight times larger.

In this synthesis we survey four decades of work on how single-nucleotide variants in a family of ion-channel-associated loci contribute to inherited arrhythmia risk, drawing on four hundred twelve published pedigree studies and twenty-six population biobanks. A consistent picture emerges: rare loss-of-function variants inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern account for most early-onset cases, while common variants of modest effect, identified through genome-wide association approaches, appear to modulate penetrance within carrier families rather than cause disease on their own. We further discuss how variant reclassification, prompted by expanding segregation data in extended pedigrees, has shifted roughly one in six 'likely pathogenic' calls to uncertain significance.

We present a new fiber-fed spectrograph coupled to a 1.2-meter telescope, designed to obtain sub-millikelvin radial-velocity precision for confirming transiting exoplanet candidates flagged by our transit-survey pipeline. Candidate light curves are first screened by a convolutional neural network trained to distinguish planetary transits from stellar variability and instrumental artifacts, reducing follow-up spectroscopy time by roughly sixty percent. Across the first observing season, the instrument confirmed eleven sub-Neptune companions around nearby M dwarfs and measured orbital eccentricities precise enough to constrain tidal circularization timescales for the closest-in planets.

We introduce a new lightweight detection pipeline for identifying defects on high-speed manufacturing lines.

- Problem: existing inspection cameras miss small surface defects when belt speed exceeds 2 m/s, causing costly downstream recalls.
- Approach: a two-stage convolutional network first proposes candidate regions on each frame, then a lightweight classifier head scores each region for defect type (scratch, dent, discoloration) in under 8 milliseconds.
- Training data: 340,000 labeled frames collected from six factory lines across three countries, covering metal, plastic, and painted surfaces under varying lighting.
- Architecture: a MobileNet-style backbone with depthwise separable convolutions, pruned to run on an embedded GPU mounted above the conveyor belt.
- Augmentation: random brightness, motion blur, and synthetic occlusion were added during training to mimic real factory lighting and belt vibration.
- Results: mean average precision of 91.4% at the target frame rate, a 14-point improvement over the previous rule-based edge-detection system it replaces.
- Deployment: the model now runs in real time on all six pilot lines, flagging defective units for manual review before they reach packaging.
- Limitation: performance drops on highly reflective chrome surfaces, where glare still confuses the region-proposal stage roughly one time in twenty.
- Next steps: we are collecting additional chrome-surface frames and testing a polarization-filter camera to address the remaining failure mode before full plant rollout.

In this paper we build a mathematical model for how a small fish population changes inside a lake when a new predator bird begins to hunt there every winter. We use equations that describe birth rate of the fish, the rate they are eaten, and how much food is inside the lake for them, and we solve the equations for many different values of the bird's hunting success. When the bird eats more than around thirty percent of the young fish each winter, our model predict the fish number will fall very fast in only four or five years and then it become very hard to come back, even if the bird go away again later. This is because when fish number is low, the mother fish also produce less eggs than before, this is a effect we add to the model that make the collapse worse. We also test what happen if there is a second, smaller lake connected by a stream, so some fish can escape there when the bird come to hunt. Our result show this second lake very much helps, even small connection reduce the chance of big collapse by more than half in our simulation. We think this is important because many lake in the north of our country have only one connected water body, and if a new predator arrive, like what is happening with this bird species in recent years, the fish inside could disappear before anyone notice, unless a second lake or stream is nearby for them to use during the worst hunting months.
recorded from 40 neurons in the hippocampus while rats ran a maze, found firing rate of place cells dropped by half after we blocked NMDA receptors localy with muscimol.

We compiled grain-size and mineral composition data from 3,400 sediment cores across the continental shelf and ran cluster analysis to classify depositional environments. Four distinct facies emerged, separating turbidite-fed slope deposits from storm-reworked shelf sands. Radiometric dating of interbedded ash layers constrains the youngest facies transition to roughly 11,000 years before present, coinciding with the regional sea-level stillstand.

Over the course of eleven weeks we travelled to seventeen commercial diving stations along the northern coast to evaluate several hundred saturation divers who had each logged, on average, more than four thousand cumulative hours below sixty metres across careers spanning fifteen to thirty years, and we administered to each participant a standardized battery consisting of a fifteen-word list recall task performed immediately and again after a twenty-minute delay, a finger-tapping speed test performed with both the dominant and non-dominant hand, and a simple reaction-time task in which participants pressed a button as soon as a light on a small handheld unit changed from red to green. At nine of the seventeen stations, where a portable scanner happened to be available through a partnership with the regional hospital, we additionally obtained structural imaging of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal and temporal regions in a subset of ninety-four divers who volunteered for the extra thirty-minute session. Across the full sample, divers with more than five thousand cumulative hours showed a consistent and fairly steep decline in delayed word recall relative to divers with under a thousand hours, even after we statistically accounted for age, years of formal education, and self-reported alcohol use, and among the subset who underwent the additional scanning session, the steepness of that decline tracked closely with measurable thinning of the same white matter pathways, suggesting the two sets of findings are connected through a common underlying process that professional divers along this coast may be quietly accumulating over the length of an ordinary career.

We analyze a large materials database comprising over 18,000 experimentally characterized alloy compositions and their corresponding tensile strength, hardness, and fatigue life measurements, in order to identify which combinations of alloying elements most reliably improve mechanical performance without compromising ductility. Using gradient-boosted regression trained on this dataset, we find that small additions of niobium and vanadium consistently raise yield strength across nearly all steel families studied, while excessive chromium content beyond twelve percent by mass tends to embrittle the microstructure regardless of heat treatment. The resulting predictive model, now deployed internally, has already guided the design of two new alloy candidates currently undergoing physical testing.

okay so field trip #3 to the mountain villages was WILD lol. we spent like 12 days going village to village (nine villages total, some literally only reachable by a footpath that our guide called 'a bit muddy' which is the understatement of the century) recording elders saying the same 200-word list over and over so we could compare how each village pronounces stuff differently. ngl by day 4 my recorder app crashed twice and i almost cried but we got like 1,100 minutes of audio total which is insane. the fun part came after: we fed all the pronunciation differences into this phylogenetic tree software that's literally built for figuring out how species are related evolutionarily (shoutout to my bio major roommate for suggesting it lmaooo) and just repurposed it to build a family tree of the nine village varieties based on how many sound changes separate them. and it WORKED so well?? the tree it spat out basically matches the old trade-route map from like 300 years ago, the villages that were connected by the old salt road cluster together on the tree, and the two villages separated by that giant ridge are the most divergent branches even though they're only 8km apart as the crow flies. our advisor was skeptical the borrowed software would even run on our kind of data but honestly the output made way more sense of the sound-change patterns than anything we tried by hand. next step is going back for a fourth village that got skipped because of a landslide, apparently they still use an older form of three consonants that dropped out everywhere else, which if true would make that branch even more interesting.

We build a new drill for taking ice from deep under the polar ice sheet, that make less melting while it cut, so the air bubble trapped inside stay clean for testing later. Old drills often heat the ice too much and gas can escape before we measure it; our new design use a rotating blade with cooling fluid instead of only heat-drilling like before. We test the drill on a site where ice is very old, more than 700,000 years in the deep part, and we successful bring up a core of 2.1 kilometer without big crack. When we check the gas trapped in bubble from different depth, the amount of one gas go up and down together with how warm or cold that time period was, and this pattern repeat many time down the whole core.

This review synthesizes two decades of spectroscopic surveys of type Ia supernovae, consolidating light-curve and redshift measurements from over 3,000 events to refine constraints on the dark energy equation of state.
randomised 600 households to recieve bed nets or not, tracked malaria incidence over 18 months, net group had 42% fewer confirmed cases.

- exposed soil mesocosms to 620 ppm CO2 for one growing season
- respired carbon output rose 19% versus ambient-air controls

This brief review considers thirty years of literature on the protective oxide layers that form spontaneously on aluminium alloys, and concludes that alloying with a modest fraction of magnesium yields the most durable such layer under marine exposure.

So we finally got round to running the full synthesis we'd been planning for months, and honestly it went better than any of us expected! Starting from a cheap, commercially available cyclohexanone derivative, we ran a three-step sequence: first a Grignard addition to install the side chain, then a Jones oxidation to bring the new alcohol back up to a ketone, and finally an intramolecular aldol condensation to close the six-membered ring and give us the target bicyclic enone. The Grignard step was a little finicky at first, our yields kept stalling around 40% until we switched from diethyl ether to THF as solvent and cooled the addition down to minus twenty degrees, after which conversion jumped up to 81% by GC. The oxidation was clean as always, Jones reagent rarely lets us down there, but the aldol closure took some coaxing: we tried three different bases (DBU, piperidine, and sodium ethoxide) before piperidine in refluxing ethanol gave us a workable 65% isolated yield after column chromatography. We confirmed the final structure by a full set of NMR experiments plus high-resolution mass spec, and everything lines up beautifully with the proposed enone, including the diagnostic vinyl proton around 5.9 ppm that we'd been hoping to see since we first drew this molecule on a napkin at a conference dinner two years ago. Next we're planning to test whether the enone will undergo a clean Diels-Alder with a couple of dienes we have sitting in the freezer, fingers crossed it behaves as nicely as the rest of the route has so far.

- Source: two years of overhead camera feeds from 40 grocery stores, sampled at one frame per second.
- Task: draw a box around each shopping cart in every frame and count how many cross the checkout threshold per hour.
- Scale: 1.1 billion frames processed, split across an 80/20 train/holdout partition by store.
- Finding: counts derived from the frame-by-frame boxes matched manual register logs within 3% at 38 of 40 stores.
- Outlier stores: two locations with low ceiling height produced more missed boxes due to camera angle.

We report the commissioning of a new silicon pixel detector for the inner tracking layer of a hadron collider experiment, achieving a single-hit spatial resolution of 8 microns. Initial beam tests confirm stable operation at instantaneous luminosities up to 2x10^34 cm^-2 s^-1, with radiation tolerance validated to an integrated fluence of 5x10^15 neutron-equivalents per square centimeter, sufficient for the full high-luminosity run.

We field-deployed a portable X-ray fluorescence probe for rapid, non-destructive elemental logging of outcrop mineral zonation, cutting stratigraphic-section characterization time from days of lab prep to a single afternoon.

So between school pickup and making dinner I finally got a minute to look at the reaction-yield database we've been building all year, and basically we pulled together results from over 2,200 esterification reactions run across our whole lab group and just threw them into a spreadsheet to see which catalyst and solvent combos actually gave the best conversion, and it turns out the para-toluenesulfonic acid runs in toluene beat literally everything else we tried by a solid ten to fifteen percent average yield, which honestly I should've guessed months ago but between grading labs and my kid's soccer practice I never had time to sit down and crunch the numbers until now.

My father used to tell this story about the time he missed his own brother's wedding because of a broken-down car on the interstate, stuck for six hours in the middle of nowhere with nothing but a bag of pretzels and a map he couldn't fold back up properly, and somehow that story comes to mind every single time I sit down to write one of these literature reviews, because writing a synthesis always feels like being stuck somewhere with no clear way forward until suddenly, usually around hour four, something clicks. This time the topic was measles resurgence in regions with historically high vaccination coverage, and I want to say up front that gathering the sources was its own adventure — half the older regional health bulletins from the 1990s only exist as scanned PDFs with terrible OCR, so I spent an embarrassing number of evenings squinting at documents that read like ransom notes, missing letters everywhere, dates that clearly said '1994' rendered as '1997' by whatever scanner they used decades ago. Anyway, after wrangling forty-one studies spanning six countries into something coherent, the throughline that emerged across nearly all of them was that outbreaks tend to cluster tightly around localized pockets of unvaccinated individuals rather than being explained by any broad decline in population-level immunity, meaning the aggregate coverage statistics that health departments love to publish can look perfectly reassuring on paper while masking exactly the kind of geographic clustering that lets a single imported case ignite a chain of dozens more within weeks. My father, incidentally, did eventually make it to the wedding, four hours late and smelling like pretzels, and everyone forgave him within about a day.

Between shuttling the kids to practice and trying to get dinner on the table I've been chipping away at this dataset from the last detector run, something like two hundred million collision events we recorded over the spring, and I finally ran the full selection cuts isolating events with two high-momentum muons and a missing transverse energy signature, and after background subtraction there's this small but pretty persistent bump sitting around 125 GeV in the invariant mass spectrum that keeps showing up no matter how I slice the cuts, which is exciting enough that I've been staying up later than I should trying to nail down the systematic uncertainties before anyone else on the team sees it.

My neighbor Frank has this ongoing argument with his brother-in-law about whether the winters here are actually getting milder or if it's 'just Frank getting soft,' as his brother-in-law likes to say every Thanksgiving without fail, and this argument has apparently been running for something like fifteen years now, complete with Frank keeping a handwritten logbook of the first frost date every single year taped to the inside of his garage door. I think about that logbook a lot, actually, because it's a weirdly good example of the kind of noisy, single-location data that makes our job so much harder than people assume. Anyway, this quarter I've mostly been buried in committee work — we spent an entire six-hour meeting last month just arguing about the new printer budget, which somehow turned into a debate about whether the break room coffee machine needed replacing, and I genuinely thought we'd adjourn without deciding anything, we did not, the coffee machine is being replaced — but in between all that I did manage to finish the coupled ocean-atmosphere energy-balance model I've been building, where the ocean mixed-layer depth now responds dynamically to wind stress instead of being held fixed like in the older version, and running it forward under a doubled-CO2 scenario the model's equilibrium warming came out about 0.6 degrees higher than the fixed-depth version predicted, mostly because the shallower effective mixed layer in summer months responds faster to the same radiative forcing. Frank, for the record, remains convinced it's just him getting soft, and I have decided not to send him the model output, some arguments are better left unresolved over turkey.

Our six-person field team departed from the trailhead at what our itinerary rather optimistically described as 0600 hours, though in practice we did not actually assemble all six pieces of camping equipment, seventeen sample bags, two working GPS units, and Marguerite's inexplicably heavy cast-iron skillet into the two support vehicles until closer to 0740, a delay that set the tone, frankly, for the entire eleven-day expedition into the upper canyon system. The first three days were consumed almost entirely by logistics of a kind that will be tediously familiar to anyone who has organized a remote survey: negotiating access with two separate ranching families whose land bordered the access road, replacing a blown tire on the supply truck using a jack that turned out to be rated for a substantially lighter vehicle, and waiting out an unseasonal two-day rainstorm inside a canvas mess tent that, despite everyone's best efforts at reinforcement, leaked steadily onto the exact corner where we had unwisely stored the reference maps. Evenings were spent, as they always are on these trips, debating the relative merits of instant versus 'real' coffee, a debate I will not relitigate here except to say that Desmond's instant-coffee advocacy remains, in my considered opinion, indefensible. It was not until day six that conditions allowed us to reach the target exposure, where we spent a single, intensely productive afternoon measuring strike and dip across the exposed fault scarp and collecting oriented samples from six discrete vein-fill generations, finding that the youngest calcite veins cut consistently across the older quartz-filled fractures at a steep, unrelated angle, indicating at least two distinct episodes of fracture reactivation separated by a substantial interval of quiescence. The remaining five days of the expedition were, in the interest of full disclosure, spent almost entirely on the return hike, which took considerably longer than planned owing to a washed-out section of trail and Marguerite's insistence, vindicated in the end, on carrying the skillet the entire way rather than caching it as the rest of us had suggested.

Our latest sky survey run flagged nine 'new' transient sources, eight of which turned out to be satellite glints once we cross-checked the orbital catalogs, and the ninth is, we are cautiously prepared to admit, an actual nova.
We excluded herbivores from half of forty grassland plots for two growing seasons and measured a 34% increase in plant species richness inside the exclosures relative to grazed controls.

ok so we built this numerical model of how magma actually moves up through a volcano's plumbing before it erupts, and it's honestly kind of wild lol. basically we simulate the pressure building up in the magma chamber and how cracks propagate through the overlying rock as it pushes upward, and the model predicts eruption onset within about six hours of when three real historical eruptions actually happened, which is way better than we expected tbh. def feels like a big step for eruption forecasting.

We had forty participants read the same sentence aloud under three stress conditions and timed which syllables shortened first; fatigue erodes rhythm from the edges of a phrase inward, not, as one confident undergraduate insisted, 'basically at random.'

between drop-off and lunch break I squeezed in checking last night's spectrograph data, and the absorption lines in that white dwarf's spectrum are shifted just enough that it's got a low-mass companion tugging on it, gotta run before pickup though.

In this modest contribution we present a computational model of synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal CA1 region, wherein long-term potentiation is governed by a calcium-dependent learning rule calibrated against decades of electrophysiological recordings. The model reproduces, with gratifying fidelity, the well-documented dependence of potentiation magnitude upon stimulation frequency, and we venture to hope it may prove a useful scaffold for future investigators.

My daughter came home last spring using a word I had genuinely never heard before, something like 'mid' to mean unimpressive, and when I asked where on earth she'd picked it up she just looked at me like I'd asked what a phone was, which is roughly how this whole project got started. We ended up building a corpus of about eleven million anonymized text messages donated by volunteers across four age brackets, spanning nine years, and tracking a set of two hundred slang terms from the moment each one first appears in the data through to whatever eventually happens to it. Most terms follow a pretty predictable arc: a sharp uptake among the youngest cohort, a lag of roughly eighteen months before the term starts showing up meaningfully in the messages of adults, and then, for the large majority, a slow fade back out of use within three to four years as new terms crowd them out. A handful of terms break that pattern entirely, though, spreading almost simultaneously across all four age brackets within a matter of weeks, and when we looked closer, nearly every one of those simultaneous-spread terms had been used first in a viral video or a widely shared clip rather than emerging organically within the youngest cohort's own messaging network, which suggests something different is going on mechanically for terms that ride in on shared media versus ones that diffuse the old-fashioned way, person to person. My daughter, for what it's worth, has already declared 'mid' itself thoroughly outdated, which tracks with the eighteen-month curve almost exactly, though she was distinctly unimpressed when I pointed that out to her.

Spent the week hiking to our string of alpine snowpack stations, and I'll be honest, it was a little unsettling how much earlier the snowline had retreated up-slope compared to our readings from just five years ago at the same stations!

It has been the present writer's privilege, over some four decades in this field, to observe the maturation of asymmetric catalysis from a scattering of promising but capricious results into what may fairly be called a mature discipline, and this review attempts, in the space allotted, to trace that maturation through the lens of enantioselective conjugate addition reactions specifically. One must acknowledge, in fairness to the younger generation of practitioners, that the recent enthusiasm for machine-learning models trained to predict enantiomeric excess from a catalyst's structural descriptors has produced some genuinely striking results, with several groups now reporting that trained models can shortlist promising chiral ligands faster than a graduate student could screen them by traditional trial and error. This reviewer does not dismiss such tools; indeed, he finds them rather useful for narrowing an otherwise unwieldy search space. But it would be a disservice to the field to suggest, as certain enthusiastic conference talks have implied, that the underlying chemistry has thereby become a solved problem. The stubborn cases remain stubborn: substrates bearing a coordinating heteroatom adjacent to the reacting centre continue to defeat even the best-predicted ligands with dispiriting regularity, and the mechanistic question of precisely how the chiral copper complex discriminates between prochiral faces of the enone substrate remains, four decades on, only partially resolved. It is this reviewer's considered judgment, offered with the mild impatience of age, that the field's future progress will depend rather more on careful mechanistic study of these recalcitrant substrates than on any further refinement of the predictive models now so fashionable.

This review surveys a decade of searches for supersymmetric partners at proton-proton colliders, most of which now rely on deep neural network classifiers to separate rare signal events from overwhelming jet backgrounds. Despite the improved background rejection these classifiers provide, no statistically significant excess consistent with gluino or squark production has emerged across the full mass range probed, pushing exclusion limits for gluino masses below 2.2 TeV at 95% confidence. We conclude that near-term progress will depend less on classifier refinement than on the luminosity upgrades scheduled for the next collider run.

Procurement of the new instrument proceeded through the standard three-tier approval process: an initial capital expenditure request submitted in March, technical specification review by the facilities committee in April, and final budget sign-off in June, some eleven weeks later than originally scheduled owing to a backlog in the finance office unrelated to this project. Installation itself required coordinating three separate contractors: an electrical subcontractor to bring a dedicated 208-volt line to the bench, a certified technician from the manufacturer to calibrate the internal mass-flow controllers, and our own facilities staff to route the nitrogen supply line through the adjacent utility chase, a process that consumed the better part of two working weeks and generated a paperwork trail exceeding forty pages, all of which has now been filed appropriately in the equipment log per institutional policy. Commissioning runs using inert solvent alone occupied a further three days, confirming stable flow rates across the full range of the syringe pumps and verifying that in-line temperature control held within plus or minus half a degree across a six-hour continuous run. With the system fully commissioned, we then used the continuous-flow reactor to carry out a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl bromide and a boronic ester under residence times of under ninety seconds, achieving 92% conversion at throughput roughly forty times higher than the equivalent batch reaction previously run in round-bottom flasks, a result that should materially shorten turnaround on the multi-step sequences this instrument was acquired to support. Ongoing maintenance will follow the standard quarterly schedule already logged in the facilities calendar, with the first service interval due in early winter.

Across thirty quadrats stratified by distance from the river channel, our floodplain-forest transect survey documented a robust decline in seedling density with distance from the water's edge, plausibly reflecting the underlying soil-moisture gradient.

ran the full f2 cross this month, 340 pups total from 22 litters, and honestly the part that ate the most time wasnt the breeding itself, it was scoring coat color. we trained a little image classifier on photos of each pup's back to sort them into the three expected color classes automatically instead of us squinting at every single pup under the same bad fluorescent light in the mouse room, which saved a ton of hours and the classifier agreed with our manual calls on like 97% of pups we double checked by hand. but the actual point of the cross was testing whether the coat locus and the newer tail-kink locus we mapped last year segregate independently or are linked. counted up all 340 pups by genotype at both markers (ran pcr and gel on tail snips for every single one, that part took foreverr) and the recombinant classes came out at about 9% of the total instead of the 25% youd expect if the loci were unlinked, which is a pretty clear signal theyre sitting close together on the same chromosome, maybe 9 cm apart based on the recombination frequency. gonna redo the pcr genotyping on a subset just to make sure we didnt mess up any samples during the tail-snip extraction, we had a couple tubes get mislabeled last time and dont want that messing up the map distance estimate. if this holds up it'll be worth pushing the fine-mapping further since 9 cm is tight enough that a candidate gene search in that interval is actually doable now.

Every few years another paper promises that a deep-learning model trained on satellite imagery will finally replace the fieldwork of mapping landslide hazard, and every few years the promise turns out somewhat oversold. This review works through fourteen such studies and finds the models perform best in terrain field geologists had already characterized by hand — steep slopes with known weak bedding-plane orientations and a history of translational slides — and worst in the ambiguous terrain that actually needed the help, where colluvium sits atop fractured bedrock near the internal friction limit and no surface texture in a photo tells you what's happening ten meters down. Bedrock structure and pore-water pressure at depth still decide whether a slope fails, and no classifier trained on pixels from above has found a way around that.

This synthesis draws together sixty-three field studies published over the past twenty-five years examining how the removal of a single apex predator reshapes the structure of the ecosystems it once occupied. Across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine systems alike, a consistent pattern emerges: mid-sized predator populations released from top-down suppression tend to expand rapidly, often within two to four years of the apex predator's local disappearance, and this expansion in turn drives measurable declines in the smaller prey species those mesopredators consume. The magnitude of the effect varies considerably by system productivity; the most severe cascades, involving order-of-magnitude shifts in prey abundance, occur disproportionately in low-productivity systems where alternative prey resources for the expanding mesopredator population are scarce. High-productivity systems tend to buffer the cascade, since mesopredators there have enough alternative food sources that they do not need to concentrate foraging pressure so intensely on any single prey population. We also find that recovery, when the apex predator is eventually reintroduced or allowed to recolonize naturally, is neither guaranteed nor symmetric with the original collapse: in roughly a third of the reviewed cases, the ecosystem settled into an alternative stable configuration that persisted for a decade or more after the predator's return, with mesopredator populations remaining elevated and prey populations remaining suppressed relative to pre-removal baselines. This asymmetry between collapse and recovery timelines carries direct implications for how conservation programs plan and evaluate predator-reintroduction efforts, since a simple return of the missing species to the landscape does not by itself guarantee that the rest of the community will follow it back to its earlier configuration.

We had so much fun building this one! We put together a population-genetics model that tracks how a beneficial allele spreads through a species when it's tightly linked to a nearby harmful mutation, essentially riding along despite the fitness cost of its neighbor. Running the simulation across a huge range of recombination rates, we found the beneficial allele still sweeps to fixation surprisingly often as long as recombination breaks the linkage within about fifty generations, which honestly surprised even us.

ok so we built this new self-healing coating for aluminum panels and it's actually so cool. basically we mix in these microcapsules full of a resin that pops open and seals a scratch the second it forms, no waiting around. we used a little computer-vision script to scan the panels after each scratch test and count how many micro-cracks actually sealed up vs stayed open, which honestly made grading way faster than someone squinting at panels with a magnifying glass all day. but the real result is the coating itself: 89% of scratches under 200 microns wide sealed fully within six hours at room temp, no heat treatment needed, which beats every microcapsule coating we've read about so far. next we wanna see if it holds up after like fifty freeze-thaw cycles.

This review traces the evolution of image classification architectures over the past decade, from early convolutional networks trained on modest labeled datasets to the large-scale vision transformers now dominant in the field. We observe that gains in top-1 accuracy on standard image benchmarks have slowed considerably since 2021, even as model parameter counts have continued to grow, suggesting the field may be approaching diminishing returns from scale alone absent new architectural insight.

We analyze twelve year of camera trap data from 84 forest site to look how deer number change after wolf come back to the region. The data include almost two million photo, and we count how many time deer appear at each site per month as a way to estimate their number without catching any animal. After wolf established territory near a site, deer photo rate drop by about 40 percent within three year, but only at site close to open meadow, not inside dense forest, which we think is because deer avoid open area more when predator is near.

Between packing lunches and helping with math homework I've been slowly chipping away at this modeling project all semester, and it's finally starting to come together, which feels like a small miracle given how little uninterrupted time I actually get most days, but the basic idea is that we're simulating how a disk of gas and dust around a young star gradually clumps together into planet-sized bodies over a few million years, tracking how particles collide and stick or shatter depending on their relative speed and size, and running the whole thing forward from an initially smooth, well-mixed disk, and what keeps surprising me every time I rerun it with slightly different starting conditions is how sensitive the final outcome is to the disk's initial turbulence level, because a slightly more turbulent starting disk pushes particle collision speeds up just enough that things shatter instead of stick for an extra half million years or so, which delays the whole planet-formation process by an amount that seems small on paper but actually shifts which parts of the disk end up hosting rocky planets versus where the gas giants form later on, and I keep thinking about how weird it is that something as chaotic and messy as turbulence, which I frankly deal with plenty of at home already, turns out to be one of the biggest levers on whether a system like ours ends up with anything like an Earth in it at all.

In this paper we propose a new theoretical model for explain how children learn the grammar rule of their first language without receive explicit correction most of the time from their parent. We build on the idea that children have some built-in bias toward simpler grammar structure, and we make a computer simulation where a learner agent hear many sentence from a artificial language with different possible rule, and the agent must guess which rule is correct one based only on the sentence it hear, not from any feedback about right or wrong. Our simulation show that when we give the learner agent this simplicity bias, it converge to the correct grammar rule much faster than a learner agent that treat all possible rule as equally likely at the start, matching more close what we know about how real child acquire syntax within just a few year of age. We also test what happen when the input language have some exception to the main rule, like irregular verb form that dont follow the pattern, and here the simplicity-biased learner sometime overgeneralize the main rule onto the exception first, producing error like 'goed' instead of 'went', before eventually learning the exception too, which is exactly the kind of error that real children also produce at this age, so this give us some confidence the model is capturing something true about how first-language grammar get acquired, not just producing a mathematically convenient result. Future work should test whether the same simplicity bias can also explain how children learn word order rule, which we did not include in the present model but believe would extend naturally from the current framework using similar assumption about learner bias.

We develop a new small device that can read DNA sequence directly in the field, without need to bring sample back to a laboratory with big machine. The device is size of a mobile phone and use a nanopore technology to pass single strand of DNA through very small hole and detect which base go through based on change in electrical current. We test the device on samples from 30 wild plant in different location, and it correctly identify the species for 27 of them within one hour of collecting the sample, compare to normal method that take several day for come back from lab. Battery only last for about four hour of continuous use so far, which limit how much we can test in one single field trip, but we hope future version can improve this.
